> This page compares all of my populations. Every number in it is read from the results files (`results/*.csv`) that the individual analyses save, so it updates when I re-run them. The reusable code lives in `R/functions.R`. Each population has its own page (`01_...md` to `06_...md`), and you can try any n yourself in the [Interactive Sampling Distribution Explorer](https://nprodhuturi.github.io/clt-monte-carlo/interactive/explorer.html).

## 1. What I investigated

The Central Limit Theorem (CLT) says that the average of many independent observations is approximately normal. The question is **how many is "many"**, and a common rule of thumb says n = 30. I tested this with a **Monte Carlo simulation**: for each population and each sample size n, I repeated the same experiment 10,000 times (B = 10,000 repetitions). In each repetition I drew a sample of n observations and recorded its mean. The 10,000 sample means approximate the sampling distribution of the mean, and I measured how close to normal it is using histograms, Q–Q plots, skewness, excess kurtosis, and a comparison of the simulated standard error with the theoretical σ/√n. I did this for every n from 1 to 40 and for n = 45, 50, 75 and 100.

I called a sample size **approximately normal** when all four of these hold (defended in [01_standard_normal.md](01_standard_normal.md)):

1.  The histogram is bell-shaped and the Q–Q plot is close to the line.
2.  \|skewness\| ≤ 0.25.
3.  \|excess kurtosis\| ≤ 0.5.
4.  The simulated standard error is within 5% of the theoretical σ/√n.

My answer for each population is the **smallest n that passes and stays passing** for every larger n I tested.

```{r}
#| label: load
source("R/setup.R")
source("R/functions.R")

files <- sort(list.files("results", pattern = "^0[1-9]_.*\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE))
prefix <- substr(basename(files), 1, 2)
res <- lapply(files, read.csv)
names(res) <- prefix

info <- data.frame(
  prefix = c("01", "02", "03", "04", "05", "06", "07", "08"),
  population = c("Standard Normal", "Six-sided die", "Exponential(1)",
                 "Binomial(5, 0.10)", "Cauchy(0, 1)", "Non-identical Bernoulli",
                 "Dependent failure", "Life / death mixture"),
  observation = c(
    "Already normal at every n (my control case).",
    "Symmetric, but flat-topped: light tails (kurtosis) held it back.",
    "Strongly skewed, so skewness decays slowly. 30 is not enough.",
    "Skewed and discrete; about 30.",
    "Mean of n Cauchy values is Cauchy again, so no n works.",
    "Changing probabilities barely mattered: almost the same as a constant 0.70.",
    "See its own page.",
    "See its own page."
  )
)
info <- info[info$prefix %in% prefix, ]
```

## 2. Summary table

```{r}
#| label: table
get_row <- function(p) {
  r <- res[[p]]
  r$good <- flag_good(r)
  if (p == "05") {
    r$good <- FALSE
  }
  ns <- smallest_good_n(r)
  if (is.na(ns)) {
    return(data.frame(n_star = NA, skew = NA, kurt = NA, sd_ratio = NA))
  }
  row <- r[r$n == ns, ]
  data.frame(n_star = ns, skew = row$skewness, kurt = row$excess_kurtosis,
             sd_ratio = row$sd_ratio)
}
rows <- do.call(rbind, lapply(info$prefix, get_row))
summary_table <- data.frame(
  Population = info$population,
  `Smallest n judged normal` = ifelse(is.na(rows$n_star), "none", rows$n_star),
  `Skewness at that n` = ifelse(is.na(rows$skew), "-", sprintf("%.3f", rows$skew)),
  `Excess kurtosis at that n` = ifelse(is.na(rows$kurt), "-", sprintf("%.3f", rows$kurt)),
  `SD ratio at that n` = ifelse(is.na(rows$sd_ratio), "-", sprintf("%.3f", rows$sd_ratio)),
  `Key observation` = info$observation,
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(summary_table, row.names = FALSE)
```

The SD ratio is the simulated standard error divided by the theoretical σ/√n, so 1 means a perfect match. The Cauchy has no σ, so its row has no values.

## 3. Larger research questions

### 3.1 Is there a universal rule such as n = 30?

```{r}
#| label: universal
ns <- rows$n_star[!is.na(rows$n_star)]
n30_too_big  <- sum(ns < 30)
n30_too_small <- sum(ns > 30)
```

**No.** Across the populations where the CLT works, the selected n runs from `r min(ns)` to `r max(ns)`, and for the Cauchy there is no n at all. Of the `r length(ns)` populations that reach approximate normality, `r n30_too_big` need fewer than 30 observations (so 30 is wasteful) and `r n30_too_small` needs more than 30 (so 30 is not enough). The Cauchy never works. So n = 30 is **too many for some, too few for others, and not helpful for heavy tails**. What matters is the shape of the population, not a fixed number.

### 3.2 Which populations converged fastest and slowest, and why?

**Fastest:** the Normal (n = `r rows$n_star[info$prefix == "01"]`) and the die (n = `r rows$n_star[info$prefix == "02"]`). The Normal is already normal. The die is symmetric and has no long tail, so it only needed a little averaging to fix its flat top.

**Slowest (among those that converge):** the Exponential (n = `r rows$n_star[info$prefix == "03"]`). **It never converges at all for the Cauchy.**

**Why:** the sample mean's skewness shrinks like the population skewness divided by √n. A skewed population needs n large enough to push that below my 0.25 limit:

```{r}
#| label: why
pop <- c("01", "02", "03", "04")
pop <- pop[pop %in% info$prefix]
pop_skew <- sapply(pop, function(p) res[[p]]$skewness[res[[p]]$n == 1])
predicted <- (abs(pop_skew) / 0.25)^2
why <- data.frame(
  Population = info$population[match(pop, info$prefix)],
  `Population skewness (n = 1 row)` = round(pop_skew, 2),
  `Predicted n from skewness alone` = ceiling(predicted),
  `Selected n` = rows$n_star[match(pop, info$prefix)],
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(why, row.names = FALSE)
```

The predicted n is (population skewness / 0.25)². It is close to the selected n for the skewed populations (Exponential, Binomial). For the die, which has no skewness at all, it predicts 1 but the selected n is larger, because light tails (kurtosis) decided it instead. So **the more skewed the population, the larger n needs to be**, and symmetric populations converge fastest.

### 3.3 Assumptions

The CLT has assumptions: the observations should be independent, come from the same distribution, and have a finite variance. I broke each of them to see what happens.

**Observations that are not identically distributed (file 06).** In the basketball example, the chance of making a shot fell from 0.90 to 0.50 during the game, so the shots were not identical. The CLT still worked. The selected n was 12, almost the same as the 14 I got for a shooter with a constant 0.70 chance. The one thing I had to change was the formulas for the mean and standard error, because every shot has its own probability. So being identically distributed is not strictly needed, but independence still is.

```{r}
#| label: cauchy
c5 <- res[["05"]]
```

**Extremely heavy tails (file 05).** The Cauchy has no mean and no variance, and the CLT failed completely. The IQR (the spread of the middle half) of the sample means stayed between about 1.9 and 2.1 at every n, when the theory says it is exactly 2. The share of sample means beyond ±10 also stayed near 0.063 at every n. Averaging 100 Cauchy values was no better than using one value. So a finite variance is not a small technical detail; the CLT depends on it.

**Dependent observations.** `I did not complete a dependent-observation analysis in this project, so I cannot report a result for it. The standard error formula σ/√n assumes independence; with positive dependence the averages vary more than σ/√n predicts, so more observations are needed."`

## 4. How sensitive are the answers to my cutoffs?

My rule of \|skewness\| ≤ 0.25 and \|excess kurtosis\| ≤ 0.5 is a judgment call. To see how much it matters, I re-apply the same simulation results with a stricter and a looser rule (no new simulation):

```{r}
#| label: sensitivity
rule <- function(p, s, k) {
  r <- res[[p]]
  r$good <- flag_good(r, skew_max = s, kurt_max = k)
  if (p == "05") r$good <- FALSE
  ns <- smallest_good_n(r)
  if (is.na(ns)) {
    if (p == "05") "none" else "> 100"
  } else {
    as.character(ns)
  }
}
sens <- data.frame(
  Population = info$population,
  `Stricter (0.10 / 0.25)` = sapply(info$prefix, rule, s = 0.10, k = 0.25),
  `My rule (0.25 / 0.5)`   = sapply(info$prefix, rule, s = 0.25, k = 0.5),
  `Looser (0.5 / 1.0)`     = sapply(info$prefix, rule, s = 0.5, k = 1.0),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(sens, row.names = FALSE)
```

The columns give the skewness limit / kurtosis limit. A stricter rule needs larger n, and a looser rule needs smaller n, but the **ranking stays about the same**: the Normal is always fastest, the skewed populations (Exponential and Binomial) are always the slowest, and the Cauchy never passes. So the main conclusion does not depend on my exact cutoffs, but the exact n values do. The "\> 100" entries mean the rule is not met by n = 100, the largest I tested.

## 5. Overall conclusions

```{r}
#| label: sd-range
ok_files <- setdiff(names(res), "05")
all_ratio <- unlist(lapply(ok_files, function(p) {
  r <- res[[p]]
  r$sd_ratio[r$n > 1 | p != "06"]
}))
sd_lo <- min(all_ratio)
sd_hi <- max(all_ratio)
```

1.  **There is no universal n.** The number needed ranged from `r min(ns)` to `r max(ns)` for populations where the CLT works, and was undefined for the Cauchy. n = 30 is a rough guide, not a law.
2.  **Skewness is the main driver.** The more skewed the population, the larger n has to be, and the relationship roughly follows (skewness / 0.25)². Symmetric populations converge fastest.
3.  **The standard error formula σ/√n works at every n,** even when the shape is far from normal: the simulated SD divided by the theoretical SE stayed between `r round(sd_lo, 2)` and `r round(sd_hi, 2)` in every population that has a σ. The CLT is about the *shape*, not the spread.
4.  **Assumptions matter.** Identical distribution can be relaxed (file 06). Finite variance cannot be (file 05). Independence is needed for the formulas I used.
5.  **"Normal enough" is a decision.** Stricter or looser cutoffs move the selected n, so every answer comes with the rule that produced it.

## 6. How this repository is organized

- `01_...` to `06_...`: one analysis per population (`.qmd` source, `.md` page, `_files` pictures).
- `R/setup.R` and `R/functions.R`: the shared settings (seed 8120, B = 10,000, the n list) and the reusable functions.
- `results/`: the saved numbers for every population.
- `interactive/explorer.html`: the interactive page (also linked in README).
- `ai_prompts.md`: my record of how I used AI.
